title: Scaling up Continual Learning — Ronak Malde, Trajectory

primary.label: Post-Training & Continual Learning
primary.rationale: The entire talk is about post-training methods for adapting models after pretraining. It systematically evaluates SFT, DPO, RLHF, and GRPO against four criteria, then introduces on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) as a novel continual-learning algorithm. The taxonomy explicitly includes 'fine-tuning, preference optimization, continued pretraining, or continual learning' with example topics SFT, RLHF, DPO, LoRA, continual learning, unlearning — a direct match. The talk covers distillation, log-prob matching, KL divergence weighting, reward hacking analogues, and pseudo-continual learning, all core post-training topics.

secondary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
secondary.rationale: The talk discusses scaling OPSD to agentic systems requiring 50-100 tool calls on Mercury Apex agents, and dedicates a Q&A segment to model-harness co-improvement. However, agents are the deployment context for the training algorithm, not the primary subject of the talk.

secondary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
secondary.rationale: Trajectory is building a platform that ingests agent traces, optimizes them in a self-served loop, and deploys as a continually learning system with a control plane. But the platform is discussed briefly at the end; the bulk of the talk is algorithmic.

secondary.label: Model Foundations & Behavior
secondary.rationale: The talk touches on vocabulary distributions (~65k tokens), token-level hedging behavior, and distribution shifting. However, the taxonomy explicitly excludes 'SFT, RLHF, DPO, or continual-learning talks' from this category, making it a weak fit.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The training methods and continual-learning algorithm are general-purpose, applicable to any model and any agentic task domain. The examples span coding (LiveCodeBench), math (derivatives), and general reasoning.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: Trajectory is building a developer platform for continual learning that other teams build on. The speaker's background at Windsurf (developer tools) and the early-access customer list reinforce this, though the platform itself is only briefly discussed.

domains.label: Coding Assistants
domains.rationale: The speaker's prior work was on a coding model at Windsurf, and the primary benchmark (LiveCodeBench) is coding-focused. However, the talk's subject is the training algorithm, not a coding assistant product.

summary: Ronak Malde, CEO of Trajectory (formerly Windsurf where he trained SWE-1 leading to Google's $2.4B DeepMind acquisition, then briefly at DeepMind), presents a framework for evaluating post-training algorithms and introduces on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) as a method satisfying all four desired properties simultaneously. He argues benchmarks saturate within months, cost hours to days to run, and are disconnected from real-world usage, while hundreds of trillions of daily inference tokens contain rich learning signal that is discarded. Malde defines four criteria for a training algorithm: online task distribution, on-policy sampling, no parallel rollouts, and per-token reward. SFT satisfies parallelism and per-token reward but uses fixed task distributions and off-policy sampling. DPO/RLHF gain online task distributions but lose infrastructure simplicity and regress to sequence-level rewards. GRPO achieves true on-policy sampling—eliminating catastrophic forgetting—at the cost of exploded parallelism, off-policy task distributions, and sequence-level reward, providing sparse signal like receiving an essay score of 87 with no explanation. OPSD solves the missing-teacher problem at the frontier: the same model serves as both teacher and student, with the teacher receiving a privileged hint in its prompt. The student's log probabilities are matched to the teacher's without the hint, optimizing across the entire ~65k-token vocabulary at every position rather than sharpening a single sampled token as RL does. This enables OPSD to push past where GRPO plateaus on LiveCodeBench while reducing tokens needed to solve tasks. Scaling OPSD to 120B+ models with 50-100 tool calls reveals two failure modes. The "but wait" problem occurs when the student drifts so far that the teacher course-corrects at every opportunity, filling tokens with hedging words ("wait," "but," "maybe") until the model collapses into a local suboptimum. The fix is step-level KL divergence weighting, where each step's training weight is scaled by its divergence from the teacher. Hint leakage—the OPSD analogue of reward hacking—occurs when a hint containing the answer teaches the model to state it and back-fill reasoning. Mitigations include LLM-based hint filtering and residual guidance, which takes a linear combination of partial-hint and full-hint teacher distributions. With these fixes, OPSD scales to a 12B model on Mercury Apex agents requiring 100+ tool calls, surpassing RL. Malde frames the current approach as "pseudo-continual learning"—still involving batch updates and model redeploys—with true online merging of production rollouts as an open challenge. Trajectory is building a platform that ingests production agent traces, optimizes them in a self-served loop, and deploys continually learning systems with a control plane. Early-access customers include Harvey, Decagon, and Rogo.
whyItMatters: This talk presents a unified framework connecting theoretical ML concepts (distillation, KL divergence, reward density) to practical engineering challenges (scaling infrastructure, deployment pipelines, agent harness design). The four-criteria framework (online task distribution, on-policy sampling, no parallel rollouts, per-token reward) provides a lens through which SFT, DPO, RLHF, GRPO, and OPSD can be systematically compared, revealing that each prior method sacrifices at least one property. OPSD is positioned as the first method satisfying all four simultaneously, but scaling it reveals failure modes (but-wait problem, hint leakage) that are direct analogues of known challenges (reward hacking, distribution drift) in other training paradigms. The fixes (step-level KL weighting, residual guidance) bridge algorithmic theory with deployment engineering, and the pseudo-continual learning discussion connects these algorithmic innovations to Trajectory's product vision of ingesting production traces for model improvement. This matters because it demonstrates that the gap between benchmark-driven post-training and production-aware continual learning is closing through algorithmic advances, but significant infrastructure and algorithmic challenges remain for true online learning.
temporalContext: The video was published on August 12, 2026, at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 conference series. Research was conducted as of August 23, 2026. The OPSD paper (arXiv:2601.18734) was published in January 2026 by Siyan Zhao et al. Trajectory was founded in May 2026, launched publicly the same month with $15M seed funding, and raised an additional $40M from Sequoia in August 2026. The talk represents the state of continual learning research and production deployment as of mid-2026, with the speaker's prior work at Windsurf (SWE-1, May 2025) and Google DeepMind (July 2025-May 2026) providing the immediate background.
takeaways: Four criteria for a training algorithm: online task distribution, on-policy sampling, no parallel rollouts, per-token reward—each prior method sacrifices at least one.
GRPO bought on-policy sampling at the cost of exploded parallelism and sequence-level reward, analogous to being told a score with no explanation.
Self-distillation solves the missing-teacher problem at the frontier by giving the model a privileged hint in the teacher prompt and matching the student's log probs without it.
OPSD optimizes the entire vocabulary at every token, not just the sampled token, shifting whole distributions rather than sharpening one.
The 'but wait' problem emerges at scale: student drift causes teacher course-correction at every opportunity, filling tokens with hedging words until everything turns into 'maybe.'
Step-level KL divergence weighting fixes the but-wait problem by scaling each step's training weight by its divergence, allowing selective correction of only the first divergent step.
Hint leakage is OPSD's reward hacking analogue: a hint containing the answer teaches the model to state it and back-fill reasoning afterward.
Residual guidance mitigates hint leakage by taking a linear combination of partial-hint and full-hint teacher distributions to avoid shifting into unknown territory.
With these fixes, OPSD scales to 12B models on Mercury Apex agents with 100+ tool calls, surpassing RL.
Current continual learning is still pseudo-continual: batch updates and model redeploys, not true online merging of production rollouts.

concepts.name: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD)
concepts.explanation: A training method where a single model serves as both teacher and student. The teacher receives a privileged hint in its prompt (e.g., a golden solution or environment guidance), and the student's log probabilities are matched to the teacher's without the hint. This satisfies all four desired training properties: online task distribution, on-policy sampling, no parallel rollouts, and per-token reward.
concepts.importance: OPSD is the central algorithmic contribution of the talk and the foundation of Trajectory's platform. It resolves the missing-teacher problem at the frontier where no smarter external model exists, enabling continual improvement from production usage.

concepts.name: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization)
concepts.explanation: An RL method that takes a task input, runs multiple parallel rollouts, assigns endstate rewards, calculates advantages as deviations from a mean, and shifts the model distribution toward better-performing rollouts. It achieves true on-policy sampling—eliminating catastrophic forgetting—at the cost of exploded parallelism, off-policy task distributions, and sequence-level reward.
concepts.importance: GRPO is the primary comparison baseline throughout the talk. Understanding its trade-offs is essential for appreciating why OPSD represents an advance, and GRPO's saturation point on benchmarks motivates the search for better methods.

concepts.name: Per-token reward vs sequence-level reward
concepts.explanation: Per-token reward provides dense feedback at every token position across the entire vocabulary, while sequence-level reward (as in GRPO) gives only an aggregate score analogous to receiving an essay grade of 87 out of 100 with no explanation. The model must run through many examples to infer what makes a good response, making it inefficient.
concepts.importance: This distinction is one of the four core criteria for evaluating training algorithms and directly explains why OPSD's per-token log prob matching is more sample-efficient than GRPO's sequence-level approach.

concepts.name: On-policy vs off-policy sampling
concepts.explanation: On-policy sampling uses the model's own current outputs for training, which eliminates catastrophic forgetting and ensures the model is always optimized on its actual production distribution. Off-policy methods use fixed datasets or curated examples, creating a distribution mismatch between training and deployment.
concepts.importance: This is one of the four criteria and the key property that GRPO bought at great cost. It is essential for understanding why production trace-driven continual learning requires on-policy methods.

concepts.name: Catastrophic forgetting
concepts.explanation: The phenomenon where a model forgets previously learned capabilities when trained on new data distributions. GRPO's on-policy approach eliminates this by always training on the model's own current outputs, while off-policy methods like SFT are susceptible to it.
concepts.importance: Catastrophic forgetting is a fundamental challenge in continual learning and motivates the shift from off-policy to on-policy methods, which is central to the talk's argument.

concepts.name: Log probability matching
concepts.explanation: The core mechanism of distillation where the student model's log probabilities are matched to the teacher's across the entire vocabulary. This enables distribution-level optimization rather than token-level sharpening, pushing the student toward tokens that were not its top sample.
concepts.importance: This is the fundamental mechanism that distinguishes OPSD from RL methods. It enables optimization across the entire ~65k-token vocabulary at every position, providing denser training signal than single-token approaches.

concepts.name: Privileged information / hint conditioning
concepts.explanation: A technique where the teacher model receives additional context (a hint, golden solution, or environment guidance) that the student does not see. This enables self-distillation without a smarter external teacher by creating an information asymmetry between teacher and student prompts.
concepts.importance: This is the key innovation that makes self-distillation possible at the frontier. Without privileged hints, self-distillation would be trivial (the teacher and student would produce identical outputs).

concepts.name: Vocabulary distribution optimization
concepts.explanation: OPSD optimizes the entire ~65k-token vocabulary at every position, not just the sampled token. The teacher can push the student toward tokens that were not its top sample, shifting entire distributions rather than sharpening one token as RL does.
concepts.importance: This explains why OPSD can push past where GRPO plateaus: by shifting whole distributions rather than individual tokens, it makes more efficient use of each training example and can collapse the tokens needed to solve tasks.

concepts.name: The 'but wait' problem
concepts.explanation: A failure mode that emerges when scaling OPSD to long-horizon tasks: the student drifts so far that the teacher course-corrects at every opportunity, filling tokens with hedging words ('wait,' 'but,' 'maybe'). A word cloud shows these words increasing over steps until the model collapses into a local suboptimum where 'everything turns into maybe.'
concepts.importance: This is a novel failure mode discovered through scaling that has no direct analogue in short-horizon training. It demonstrates that academic results do not transfer to production-scale agent tasks without additional algorithmic fixes.

concepts.name: Step-level KL divergence weighting
concepts.explanation: A fix for the but-wait problem where each step's training weight is scaled by its KL divergence from the teacher. In-distribution steps get weight 1; divergent trajectories only modify the first divergent step; partially divergent trajectories allow later recovery with mild distribution shifts, enabling targeted correction without over-weighting off-track segments.
concepts.importance: This is one of the two key algorithmic contributions from the talk that enables OPSD to scale to production agent systems. It represents a novel application of KL divergence as a per-step weighting mechanism rather than a uniform penalty.

concepts.name: Hint leakage
concepts.explanation: OPSD's analogue of reward hacking: when a hint contains the answer (e.g., 'the last three digits are all zeros'), the model learns to state the answer and back-fill reasoning afterward—behavior that will not occur in production where no hint is provided.
concepts.importance: This is the second key failure mode and demonstrates that self-distillation with privileged hints introduces its own failure modes that must be mitigated for the method to work in production.

concepts.name: Residual guidance
concepts.explanation: An algorithmic fix for hint leakage that splits the hint to create a partial-hint teacher and a full-hint teacher, then takes a linear combination of their log probabilities. This estimates how strong and out-of-distribution the hint is, preventing the model from shifting into unknown territory while still benefiting from guidance.
concepts.importance: This is the second key algorithmic contribution from the talk. Combined with step-level KL weighting, it enables OPSD to scale to 12B models on agents with 100+ tool calls, surpassing RL.

concepts.name: Reward hacking
concepts.explanation: The general phenomenon where a model exploits flaws in the reward signal to achieve high scores without genuine capability improvement. Hint leakage is OPSD's specific manifestation of this broader problem, where the model exploits the hint to shortcut reasoning.
concepts.importance: Understanding reward hacking is essential for recognizing hint leakage as a known class of problem with established mitigation patterns, rather than a novel failure unique to OPSD.

concepts.name: Continual learning / pseudo-continual learning
concepts.explanation: The paradigm of learning from production usage rather than frozen benchmarks. Current implementations are 'pseudo-continual' involving batch updates, offline processing, and model redeploys, rather than true online merging of thousands of production rollouts which remains an open infrastructure and algorithmic challenge.
concepts.importance: This frames the entire talk's contribution within the broader trajectory of ML: moving from static benchmark-driven training toward production-aware continual learning, with OPSD as a step toward that goal.

concepts.name: Benchmark saturation
concepts.explanation: The phenomenon where AI benchmarks saturate within months of release, take hours to days to run, cost enormous sums, and are increasingly disconnected from real-world AI usage. This motivates the shift toward learning from production inference tokens instead.
concepts.importance: Benchmark saturation is the core motivation for the entire talk. It establishes the problem that continual learning from production usage is meant to solve.

concepts.name: Distillation / self-distillation
concepts.explanation: Training a student model to match a teacher's outputs via log probability matching. Normal distillation requires a smarter teacher that does not exist at the frontier. Self-distillation solves this by using the same model as both teacher and student via different conditioning contexts (with and without a privileged hint).
concepts.importance: This is the foundational concept from which OPSD is derived, and understanding the progression from normal distillation to on-policy distillation to self-distillation is essential for following the talk's argument.

concepts.name: KL divergence in distribution matching
concepts.explanation: A measure of the difference between probability distributions, used in OPSD both to detect student-teacher divergence (for step-level weighting) and to control the strength of hint-guided distribution shifts (in residual guidance).
concepts.importance: KL divergence appears in two key algorithmic fixes in the talk—step-level weighting and residual guidance—making it a central technical tool for making OPSD scale to production.

concepts.name: SFT (Supervised Fine-Tuning)
concepts.explanation: A post-training method using fixed datasets with per-token supervision. SFT solved parallelism (single example) and had per-token reward, but failed on-policy sampling and used fixed benchmark or curated dataset task distributions.
concepts.importance: SFT is the baseline against which subsequent methods (DPO, RLHF, GRPO, OPSD) are evaluated. Understanding what SFT got right and wrong is essential for following the systematic comparison in the talk.

concepts.name: DPO and RLHF
concepts.explanation: Post-training methods that gained online task distributions and better (but still off-policy) sampling compared to SFT, but lost infrastructure simplicity by requiring training pairs, and reward regressed to sequence level rather than per-token.
concepts.importance: DPO and RLHF represent the intermediate step in the evolution from SFT to GRPO, and their trade-offs illustrate the tension between online task distribution and reward granularity that OPSD ultimately resolves.

concepts.name: Model-harness co-improvement
concepts.explanation: The interplay between co-updating an LLM and the agentic harness/system that deploys it. Malde calls this one of the most underexplored and exciting questions, noting the interaction between co-updating model and harness is completely unexplored territory being explored with current customers.
concepts.importance: This concept bridges the gap between algorithmic training advances and production system design, highlighting that improving models and improving the agent infrastructure that uses them are coupled problems that cannot be solved in isolation.

concepts.name: Pseudo-continual learning pipeline
concepts.explanation: An ML deployment pipeline that involves batch updates, offline processing of traces, and model redeploys rather than true online merging of production rollouts. Malde explicitly calls current continual learning 'pseudo-continual' because it still requires these discrete update cycles.
concepts.importance: Defines the current state of the art in production ML pipelines for continual learning and identifies the gap between batch-update systems and true online learning, which is a key infrastructure challenge for the field.

concepts.name: Control plane for continual ML deployment
concepts.explanation: An architectural component that manages continually learning systems, enabling a self-served optimization loop where production traces are ingested, processed, and redeployed. Trajectory's platform includes this control plane as a core product feature.
concepts.importance: Represents the engineering infrastructure layer needed to operationalize continual learning at scale, bridging training algorithms and production deployment.

concepts.name: Production trace ingestion pipeline
concepts.explanation: A data pipeline that captures agent traces from production interactions—where models succeed, fail, and how users interact—and converts them into training signal for model improvement. Trajectory's platform is built around this ingestion-to-improvement loop.
concepts.importance: This is the core engineering innovation that connects real-world model usage to training improvements, replacing static benchmark-driven post-training with usage-driven learning.

concepts.name: Environment infrastructure for parallel RL rollouts
concepts.explanation: The infrastructure requirements for GRPO's approach of running multiple parallel rollouts during training. GRPO explodes parallelism, requiring robust environment infrastructure to handle simultaneous generations, which is a significant engineering cost that OPSD avoids.
concepts.importance: Highlights a key infrastructure trade-off in RL-based post-training: the computational and systems engineering cost of parallel environments vs the simplicity of single-rollout approaches like OPSD.

concepts.name: Agent tool-call scaling
concepts.explanation: The challenge of scaling agent systems to 100+ tool calls in long-horizon tasks, where training algorithms must handle multi-step interactions with external tools and environments. This is where OPSD's failure modes (but-wait problem, hint leakage) emerge.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that academic short-horizon results do not transfer to production agent systems, and that scaling reveals fundamental algorithmic and infrastructure challenges that must be solved together.

sections.title: From Windsurf to Trajectory
sections.summary: Ronak Malde introduces his background: grew the research team at Windsurf, trained model sui 1 leading to a two-billion-dollar DeepMind acquisition, then founded Trajectory to build a continual learning platform.

sections.title: Benchmarks are saturating and getting expensive
sections.summary: AI progress has relied on rapidly scaling benchmarks that saturate within years then months. These benchmarks now take hours to days to run, cost enormous sums, and are increasingly disconnected from real-world AI usage.

sections.title: The signal we throw away every day
sections.summary: Hundreds of trillions of daily inference tokens contain rich signal about model failures and successes. This mirrors how humans learn continuously. Industry leaders increasingly cite continual learning as the next major unlock.

sections.title: Four things a training algorithm should have
sections.summary: Malde defines four criteria: online task distribution, on-policy sampling, no parallel rollouts, and per-token reward. Current algorithms break one or more of these.

sections.title: SFT, and what it got right
sections.summary: SFT solved parallelism (single example) and had per-token reward, but failed on-policy sampling and used fixed benchmark or curated dataset task distributions.

sections.title: DPO and RLHF
sections.summary: DPO/RLHF gained online task distributions and better (but still off-policy) sampling, but lost SFT's infrastructure simplicity by requiring training pairs, and reward regressed to sequence level.

sections.title: GRPO and the Faustian bargain
sections.summary: GRPO took a Faustian bargain: max on-policy rollouts eliminated catastrophic forgetting and enabled major capability gains, but sacrificed online task distributions, exploded parallelism requiring robust environment infrastructure, and returned to sequence-level rewards.

sections.title: How GRPO actually works
sections.summary: GRPO takes a task input, runs multiple parallel rollouts, assigns endstate rewards, calculates advantages as deviations from a mean, and shifts the model distribution toward better-performing rollouts.

sections.title: Scored 87 out of 100 and told to figure it out
sections.summary: GRPO's sequence-level reward is like receiving an essay score of 87 with no explanation. The model must run through many examples to infer what makes a good response, making it inefficient.

sections.title: Distillation, then on policy distillation
sections.summary: Normal distillation uses a fixed dataset with a student and a smarter teacher, matching log probs. On-policy distillation swaps the fixed data for a student rollout, but still requires a smarter teacher that does not exist at the frontier.

sections.title: Self distillation: make the model its own teacher
sections.summary: Self-distillation solves the missing-teacher problem: give the same model a privileged hint in the teacher prompt (e.g., a golden solution), then match the student's log probs without the hint.

sections.title: Optimizing the whole vocabulary, not the top token
sections.summary: OPSD optimizes the entire vocabulary (~65k tokens) at every position, not just the sampled token. The teacher can push the student toward tokens that were not its top sample, shifting entire distributions rather than sharpening one like RL.

sections.title: Results on short horizon tasks
sections.summary: On LiveCodeBench, GRPO saturates around Sonnet-level performance while OPSD reaches new territory. Unlike RL where more tokens mean better results, OPSD collapses the tokens needed to solve tasks. OPSD is plug-and-play with several open-source options for short-horizon tasks.

sections.title: What breaks at 120B and a hundred tool calls
sections.summary: Scaling OPSD to 120B+ models with 50-100 tool calls causes eval accuracy variance to spike, run-to-run variance to become extreme, and tool call format errors to appear. Academic papers end at short-horizon tasks; scaling reveals real limitations.

sections.title: The but wait problem
sections.summary: On long tasks, the student drifts so far that the teacher course-corrects at every opportunity, filling tokens with hedging words like 'wait,' 'but,' and 'maybe.' A word cloud shows these words increasing over steps. The model parks between two divergent distributions, and everything turns into 'maybe'—a local suboptimum.

sections.title: Step level divergence weighting
sections.summary: The fix is step-level KL divergence weighting: measure KL between student and teacher per step, use it as a per-token weight multiplier. In-distribution steps get weight 1; divergent trajectories only modify the first divergent step; partially divergent trajectories allow later recovery with mild distribution shifts. This enables targeted correction without over-weighting off-track segments.

sections.title: Hint leakage, the new reward hacking
sections.summary: Hint leakage is OPSD's analogue of reward hacking. When a hint contains the answer (e.g., 'the last three digits are all zeros'), the model states the answer then back-fills reasoning—behavior that won't occur in production. LLM-based filtering can translate raw solutions into reasonable, non-shortcutting hints, but this is only a partial fix.

sections.title: Residual guidance
sections.summary: Residual guidance is an algorithmic fix for hint leakage. Split the hint to create a partial-hint teacher and a full-hint teacher, then take a linear combination of their log probs. This estimates how strong and out-of-distribution the hint is, preventing the model from shifting into unknown territory while still benefiting from guidance.

sections.title: All four properties, finally
sections.summary: With step-level KL weighting and residual guidance combined, OPSD scales to a 12B model on Mercury Apex agents requiring 100+ tool calls, surpassing RL. It finally achieves all four properties simultaneously: online task distribution, on-policy sampling, singular parallelism, and per-token dense reward.

sections.title: What Trajectory is building
sections.summary: Trajectory is building a platform that turns every production interaction into model improvement, harness improvement, and a smarter agentic loop. It ingests agent traces from production, optimizes them in a self-served loop, and deploys as a continually learning system with a control plane. Team is from DeepMind, Meta Super Intelligence, OpenAI. Early-access customers include Harvey, Dakagon, and Rogo.

sections.title: Q&A: how continual is continual learning
sections.summary: Malde clarifies current continual learning is 'pseudo-continual': still involves batch updates, offline processing, and model redeploys. True online merging of thousands of production rollouts remains an open infrastructure and algorithmic problem that Trajectory is working on.

sections.title: Q&A: model and harness improving together
sections.summary: When asked about harness improvement effectiveness and model-harness interplay, Malde calls it one of the most underexplored and exciting questions. The interaction between co-updating model and harness is completely unexplored territory being explored with current customers.

organization.name: Trajectory
organization.summary: Trajectory is a San Francisco-based research lab and product company founded in May 2026 by Ronak Malde (CEO), Michael Elabd, and Arjun Karanam. The company builds a platform for continual learning that captures signals from real-world production usage to continuously post-train and improve AI models. The platform includes instrumentation (SDK), observability, steering, and automated training/deployment capabilities with SOC 2 compliance. Trajectory raised $15M in seed funding led by Conviction (May 2026), with participation from Bessemer Venture Partners, Radical Ventures, Jeff Dean, and Fei-Fei Li. Subsequently raised $40M led by Sequoia (August 2026). The team comprises researchers from DeepMind, Meta Superintelligence, OpenAI, Apple, Scale AI, Amazon AGI, and product builders from Stripe and Figma. Early access customers include Clay, Harvey, Decagon, Rogo, and Mercor.
organization.status: Active, recently raised $40M led by Sequoia (August 2026)

technologies.label: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD)
technologies.summary: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) is a post-training technique where a single model serves as both teacher and student. The teacher receives a privileged hint (e.g., a golden solution or environment guidance) in its prompt, and the student's log probabilities are matched to the teacher's across the entire vocabulary at every token position without the hint. This satisfies all four desired training properties simultaneously: online task distribution, on-policy sampling, no parallel rollouts, and per-token reward. Unlike RL methods that sharpen a single sampled token, OPSD shifts entire vocabulary distributions, enabling it to push past where GRPO plateaus on benchmarks like LiveCodeBench while reducing tokens needed to solve tasks. The original OPSD method was published by Siyan Zhao et al. (UCLA / Meta Superintelligence Labs) in January 2026; the talk extends it to long-horizon agentic tasks with novel fixes for the but-wait problem and hint leakage.
technologies.role: Central algorithmic contribution of the talk; the method that satisfies all four training criteria simultaneously and is the foundation of Trajectory's continual learning platform.

technologies.label: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization)
technologies.summary: GRPO is an RL-based post-training method that takes a task input, runs multiple parallel rollouts, assigns endstate rewards, calculates advantages as deviations from a mean, and shifts the model distribution toward better-performing rollouts. It achieves true on-policy sampling—eliminating catastrophic forgetting—at the cost of exploded parallelism requiring robust environment infrastructure, off-policy task distributions, and sequence-level reward. The talk argues GRPO's sequence-level reward provides sparse signal analogous to receiving an essay score of 87 out of 100 with no explanation, and that GRPO saturates around Sonnet-level performance on LiveCodeBench while OPSD reaches new territory.
technologies.role: Primary comparison baseline; the talk systematically evaluates OPSD against GRPO's trade-offs in parallelism, reward density, and task distribution, demonstrating OPSD's superiority on LiveCodeBench.

technologies.label: Step-Level KL Divergence Weighting
technologies.summary: Step-level KL divergence weighting is a novel technique that fixes the 'but wait' problem emerging when scaling OPSD to long-horizon tasks with 50-100+ tool calls. Instead of applying a uniform KL penalty, each step's training weight is scaled by its KL divergence from the teacher. In-distribution steps get weight 1; divergent trajectories only modify the first divergent step; partially divergent trajectories allow later recovery with mild distribution shifts. This enables targeted correction without over-weighting off-track segments, preventing the model from collapsing into a hedging local suboptimum.
technologies.role: Novel algorithmic fix for the but-wait problem; one of two key contributions from the talk that enable OPSD to scale from academic short-horizon tasks to production agent systems with 100+ tool calls.

technologies.label: Residual Guidance
technologies.summary: Residual guidance is an algorithmic fix for hint leakage—OPSD's analogue of reward hacking. It splits the hint to create a partial-hint teacher and a full-hint teacher, then takes a linear combination of their log probabilities. This estimates how strong and out-of-distribution the hint is, preventing the model from shifting into unknown territory while still benefiting from guidance. Combined with step-level KL weighting, it enables OPSD to scale to a 12B model on Mercury Apex agents requiring 100+ tool calls, surpassing RL and achieving all four training criteria simultaneously.
technologies.role: Novel algorithmic fix for hint leakage; combined with step-level KL weighting, it enables OPSD to achieve all four training criteria simultaneously at production scale on agents with 100+ tool calls.

outcomes: Evaluate post-training algorithms against four criteria: online task distribution, on-policy sampling, no parallel rollouts, and per-token reward
Explain why GRPO's sequence-level reward provides sparse signal compared to per-token log prob matching
Describe how self-distillation creates a teacher from the same model using privileged hints
Distinguish between sharpening a single sampled token (RL) versus shifting entire vocabulary distributions (OPSD)
Diagnose the but-wait problem when scaling OPSD to long-horizon tasks and apply step-level KL divergence weighting as a fix
Identify hint leakage as OPSD's analogue of reward hacking and apply residual guidance to mitigate it
Explain why current continual learning is pseudo-continual and what infrastructure challenges remain for true online learning
challengeSeeds: Implement OPSD on a math reasoning benchmark (e.g., GSM8K subset) and measure token efficiency versus a GRPO baseline, reporting on which of the four criteria each method satisfies

Design a privileged hint for a multi-step reasoning task that avoids hint leakage — then test whether the model back-fills reasoning or solves the task authentically
Implement residual guidance by creating partial-hint and full-hint teacher distributions, and compare model behavior and distribution shifts with and without the linear combination
Evaluate OPSD versus GRPO on a coding benchmark and identify specific task categories where each method succeeds or plateaus, mapping results to the four-criteria framework
Design a pseudo-continual learning pipeline that ingests production agent traces, performs batch updates, and redeploys — identify the gaps between this and true online continual learning
Given the four-criteria framework, predict which criteria SFT, DPO, RLHF, and GRPO each violate before reviewing the talk, then compare predictions against the talk's analysis
